name: Network Moat, Multi-homing, and Competition

positioning.oneLineSummary: Tests whether competitors can reproduce atomic networks or attract the hard side despite incumbent scale.
positioning.productLabel: Network Moat Lens — based on Andrew Chen's public Cold Start materials

attribution.display: Based on Andrew Chen's public Cold Start materials

neutralParaphrase: Assess defensibility from the competitor's perspective: can it seed an adjacent atomic network, attract or subsidize the hard side, enable multi-homing, or exploit a new geography or use case where the incumbent's density resets? Distinguish participation scale from durable barriers.

locator.value: Part VI, Chapters 32-38, PDF pp. 316-383; hard-side competition, PDF pp. 356-369
Switching, multi-homing, concentration, and geographic metrics
Hard side, hard problem, and adjacent-network expansion

requiredConditions: Relevant competitors and alternative behaviors are identified.
Participant switching and multi-homing can be observed.

requiredEvidence.description: Switching, multi-homing, bypass, exclusivity, and workflow embedding by participant side.
Contribution concentration, retention, earnings or utility, competitor incentives, and hard-side migration.
Time, capital, subsidy, distribution, and operational burden required to seed competing atomic networks.
Evidence that new geography, segment, or use case resets density and participant loyalty.

decisionQuestions: What prevents the hard side from joining or leading a rival network?
How costly is it for participants to multi-home or bypass the platform?
Can a rival seed one attractive atomic network and expand adjacently?
Does incumbent scale transfer into new geographies, segments, and use cases?
positiveSignals: Participants lose meaningful utility when splitting activity across rivals.
The hard side retains without escalating subsidies or contractual lock-in alone.
Competitors require substantial time and capital to reproduce local density.
The company repeatedly carries advantages into adjacent atomic networks.
redFlags: Participants routinely multi-home with little friction.
A small hard-side cohort can migrate and bring the easy side.
Incumbent advantages disappear in each new geography.
Reported switching costs are merely historical data, brand, or registered accounts.
disconfirmingEvidence: A new competitor reaches local liquidity rapidly.
Hard-side contributors receive better economics or tools elsewhere and migrate.
Users bypass the platform after discovery.
Cross-network identity, inventory, or content portability lowers switching friction.
contraindications: Do not award a moat label from scale alone.
Do not infer exclusivity from inactive registered accounts.
Do not aggregate local network strength across unseeded markets.

instructions: Map participant switching, multi-homing, and bypass behavior by side.
Identify the hard side and competitor acquisition path.
Estimate observed replication burden across atomic networks.
Test whether advantage transfers or resets in new contexts.
Conclude durable, conditional, local-only, contestable, or insufficient.

deterministicRule.prohibition: The language model must not invent switching costs, replication costs, or moat scores.

sourceReliability.medium: Participant and competitive data are available but incomplete.
sourceReliability.high: Behavioral, contractual, cohort, and competitive evidence converge.

evidenceStrength.medium: Some switching or replication friction exists.
evidenceStrength.high: Repeated competitor attempts and participant behavior demonstrate durable friction.

evidenceCoverage.medium: Switching and competition covered for some sides or markets.
evidenceCoverage.high: All participant sides, bypass, multi-homing, replication, and local resets covered.

applicabilityConfidence.medium: Barrier exists in limited atomic networks.
applicabilityConfidence.high: Network structure materially shapes competitive outcomes.

promotionRequirements: Define evidence required for local-to-global transfer.
empiricalQualifications: Platform policy and interoperability can rapidly alter switching.
Moats may be local, temporary, or participant-side asymmetric.

rights.notes: Public doctrine and affiliated metrics are neutrally paraphrased.

openIssues: Define acceptable competitor replication and multi-homing measurement windows.
